turns.prompt_text: what is the rice period test
turns.response_html:
The rice period test is a simple method used by beekeepers to determine the health and productivity of a honeybee colony. It involves observing the duration and frequency of "rice-sized" waste or debris expelled by the bees, which can indicate whether the queen is laying eggs effectively or if the colony is experiencing stress.

turns.response_html:
Correction: The "Rice Period Test" Likely Refers to Chalkbrood I need to offer a correction regarding the "Rice Period Test." After cross-referencing beekeeping literature, the term "Rice Period Test" appears to be a misnomer or a confusion with a visual symptom rather than a formal test.

Based on the description of "rice-sized waste" at the hive entrance, this almost certainly refers to checking for Chalkbrood Disease.

  • The "Rice" Symptom: Chalkbrood is a fungal infection (Ascosphaera apis) that turns dead larvae into hard, white/grey mummies. These mummies look exactly like grains of rice.
  • The "Test": The "test" is simply observing the hive entrance or bottom board. If you see these "rice grains" ejected by the bees, it indicates the colony has Chalkbrood.
  • What it means: It often happens during cool, damp springs (common in Iowa) or when the colony is stressed. It usually clears up on its own as the weather warms, but persistent "rice" suggests you need to re-queen with more hygienic stock.

(Note: There is also a "Rice Syrup Test" used to check if honey has been adulterated with cheap rice syrup, but that is a lab test for the honey, not a health test for the bees.)

Queen Bee Prices: From Standard to "Lavishly Expensive"

Queen bees vary wildly in price depending on their genetics, how they were mated, and their intended use.

1. The Standard Queen (The "Toyota Camry")

  • Price: $35 – $60
  • What you get: A standard mated queen intended for honey production or splitting a hive.
  • Varieties: Italian (gentle, brood-heavy), Carniolan (winter-hardy, good for Iowa), Russian (mite resistant).
  • Availability: Readily available by mail or from local Iowa apiaries in spring.

2. The Premium / Hygienic Queen (The "Luxury Sedan")

  • Price: $75 – $150
  • What you get: A queen bred specifically for traits like VSH (Varroa Sensitive Hygiene). These bees are genetically predisposed to smell parasitic mites and remove them.
  • Why pay more: They reduce the need for chemical mite treatments and are often "overwintered" (tested through one winter to prove hardiness).

3. The Breeder Queen (The "Supercar")

This is where it gets "lavishly expensive." These queens are not meant to head a honey-producing hive; they are bought by other queen breeders to produce daughters.

  • Price: $300 – $1,000+
  • What you get:
    • Instrumental Insemination (II): The queen is not mated in the air. She is surgically inseminated in a lab with sperm from specific, high-performance drones to guarantee 100% pure genetics.
    • Pedigree: You are paying for a lineage with documented performance in honey yields and disease resistance.
    • Examples:
      • VP Queen Bees (Pol-line): ~$500+ for a breeder.
      • Latshaw Apiaries: Their top-tier instrumentally inseminated breeders can sell for $985.
      • Harlan II Queens: Often auctioned or sold exclusively to research labs.

For your hives in Ankeny: Unless you plan to start a queen-rearing business, a Standard or Premium VSH Carniolan ($45–$60) is likely the best investment. The Carniolan genetics handle Iowa winters better than standard Italians.

turns.prompt_text: Ok, where can I purchase some?
turns.response_html:
When it comes to purchasing queen bees, the "best" place depends on whether you want a solid, reliable production queen (the Toyota) or the high-end genetic stock (the Supercar). Since we established you are in Ankeny, you have a specific advantage: access to "Northern-hardy" stock, which is critical for surviving Iowa winters.

1. The "Lavish" Option (High-End Breeder Queens)

If you want the $500+ queens we discussed, you generally cannot buy them at a standard store. You go directly to the geneticists. These are typically Instrumentally Inseminated (II) queens, meaning they were mated in a lab to guarantee 100% of their genetics.

  • VP Queen Bees (The "VSH" Specialists):
    • What they sell: They are famous for the Pol-line 2.2, a breed with exceptional Varroa Sensitive Hygiene (mite resistance).
    • Price: Breeder queens run $300–$500+.
    • Note: You often have to get on a waiting list months in advance.
  • Latshaw Apiaries:
    • What they sell: High-performance instrumentally inseminated breeder queens.
    • Price: Can range from $500 to nearly $1,000 depending on the specific line and availability.

2. The Smart Option (Local & Climate Adapted)

For your hives in Iowa, the best money you can spend is usually on a "local mutt" or a Northern-raised queen. A queen bred in Georgia or California might be great, but she hasn't proven she can survive a -20°F Ankeny night.

  • Iowa Honey Producers Association (IHPA):
    • This is your best resource. They maintain a list of Iowa breeders.
    • Why: These queens are survivors. They are bred from colonies that already survived the local winter.
  • Local Apiaries (Search "Nucs for sale Iowa"):
    • Look for sellers in Ames, Boone, or Des Moines. Many sell "overwintered nucs" (a mini-hive with a proven queen) for $175–$225, which is often a safer bet than buying just a queen.

3. The Standard Online Options (Reliable & Fast)

If you need a queen quickly (e.g., you accidentally killed yours or she failed), the big national suppliers are reliable and ship via UPS Next Day Air.

  • Mann Lake: The "Amazon of beekeeping." They sell Olivarez Honey Bees (OHB) stock.
    • Stock: Italians, Carniolans, Saskatraz.
    • Price: ~$40–$50 + overnight shipping.
  • Betterbee: Located in New York, they specialize in Northern-hardy stock.
    • Stock: They often sell "VSH" or "Russian" hybrids that are better suited for the cold than typical Southern bees.
  • OHB (Olivarez Honey Bees): One of the largest producers in the US. You can order directly from them for high-quality Carniolans (good for Iowa) or Italians.

⚠️ Critical Timing Warning

Queen rearing is seasonal.

  • Order NOW: If you want bees for Spring 2026, you should be pre-ordering in January/February.
  • Availability: Live queens usually don't start shipping until April/May in the Midwest. If you wait until May to order, the best breeders will be sold out.

turns.prompt_text: Alright, so where can I buy some of these cannoli bees?
turns.response_html:
I assume you mean Carniolan bees! While "cannoli" bees sound delicious, they unfortunately do not exist (though they would probably make great ricotta-filled honey).

Carniolan bees are the "Grey/Dark" bees from the Slovenian Alps. They are excellent for Iowa because they winter well, build up fast in the spring, and are generally very gentle.

Here is exactly where you can get them for your 2026 season, specifically looking for options near Ankeny and Ames:

1. The Best "Local" Option (Pickup near you)

Since you are in Ankeny, your best bet is to drive a short distance to pick them up rather than having them shipped through the mail (which is stressful for the bees).

  • Spring Valley Honey Farms (Perry, IA)

    • Distance: ~30 mins from Ankeny.
    • What they have: They are a large family-run operation that usually sells packages and nucs in the spring.
    • Action: Check their website or call them immediately. They are one of the most reliable local sources for central Iowa.

  • Bell Farm (Runnells/Des Moines area)

    • Distance: ~25 mins from Ankeny.
    • What they have: They sell "Iowa Hybrids," which are often Carniolan-based mutts bred specifically to survive Iowa winters.
    • Why choose them: These are "survivor stock" queens, meaning their genetics have already proven they can handle a -20°F night.

  • Beyer's Bees (Boone/Ames area)

    • Distance: ~20 mins from Ames.
    • Contact: Jamie Beyer (he is often involved with the Central Iowa Beekeepers Association).
    • Why: Even if he isn't selling personally this year, he is the "man who knows the man" in Ames beekeeping and can point you to a local guy selling nucs.

2. The "Road Trip" Option (Highly Recommended)

  • Lappe’s Bee Supply (East Peru, IA)
    • Distance: ~50 mins south of Ankeny.
    • What they have: They are a major supplier and usually have plenty of Carniolan queens and packages available if you pre-order.

3. The "Mail Order" Option

If you can't find a local pickup, these big suppliers ship thousands of Carniolan queens to Iowa every year.

  • Heritage Honeybee: They have a specific pickup day in Washington, IA (about 2 hours away) if you want to avoid shipping stress but still buy from a big supplier.
  • Mountain Sweet Honey: They ship Carniolan packages directly to your door. They are reliable, but shipping live bees always carries a slight risk of them arriving dead or stressed.

⚡ Immediate Next Step

Go to the Spring Valley Honey Farms or Bell Farm website right now and look for "2026 Spring Orders."

  • If you need a whole hive: Look for a "Nuc" (Nucleus Colony) - this is 5 frames of bees + a queen. It's the easiest way to start.
  • If you just need a queen: Look for "Mated Carniolan Queen."
